item.title: Japan's plan to revise its three security documents lays bare ambition to speed up remilitarization: FM spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 16:44:00
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun Japan has rushed to revise its three security documents, drastically boosting military spending, developing offensive capabilities, and laying bare its ambition to speed up remilitarization. Its so-called "greatest strategic challenge" is nothing but a pretext for military expansion under the guise of defense, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press briefing on Thursday. Guo's remarks were made in response to inquiries from the Global Times regarding Japan's plan to revise its three security documents by the end of this year, namely, the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy and Defense Buildup Program. According to media reports, the revision will continue to identify China as the "greatest strategic challenge." The proposals include raising defense spending over the next five years to nearly double the amount under the current plan, with a total budget ranging from 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen ($457 billion to $508 billion). "We have noticed concerns within Japan that the nation's identity as a 'peaceful country' is eroding, with severe repercussions for its economy and people's livelihoods," said Guo. Japanese militarism committed heinous crimes in history, inflicting untold suffering on peoples across the Asia-Pacific and the world. That bitter lesson is still fresh and must not be forgotten, he added. As Japan races ahead with militarization and keeps breaking away from the "exclusively defense-oriented" principle, it poses a grave threat to regional peace and stability and challenges the postwar international order. The international community must stay highly vigilant and jointly rein in such moves, said the spokesperson. Global Times

item.title: China open to increasing US agricultural imports, contingent on 30 billion reciprocal tariff cuts: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 16:26:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China has always been open to increasing purchases of US agricultural products, but this is contingent on the implementation of the reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement covering $30 billion in trade on each side, a spokesperson of Chinese Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Thursday in response to a question about imports of US agricultural products. China-US agricultural trade is an important part of bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Expanding cooperation in agriculture would not only provide consumers in both countries with a wider variety of food products but also generate stable income for businesses and farmers on both sides, delivering tangible benefits to both countries, Huang Ling, MOFCOM spokesperson said. Huang expressed hope that the US would work with China to create more favorable conditions for bilateral agricultural trade by jointly reducing tariffs, lowering non-tariff barriers and expanding market access. Global Times

item.title: China urges EU to carefully assess impact of new fees and tariffs on low-value imports
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 16:19:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China hopes the EU will carefully assess the impact of its new policies on low-value imports and create favorable conditions for China-EU cooperation in e-commerce and other areas, Huang Ling, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce, said on Thursday. The remarks came in response to a question about the EU's introduction of a 2-euro handling fee on low-value imports starting November 1, following the implementation of a 3-euro tariff in July, and the combined impact of the two measures on Chinese cross-border e-commerce exporters. Huang said China is paying close attention to the EU's new regulations, noting that cross-border e-commerce, as a new form and model of international trade, provides businesses and consumers around the world with a diverse range of choices. Global Times

item.title: Annual CIIE opens in Shanghai, highlighting 'opportunity,' 'openness' and 'market' for global companies
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 16:06:00
This photo taken on Nov. 2, 2026 shows a view of the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), the main venue for the China International Import Expo (CIIE), in east China's Shanghai.(Xinhua/Ding Ting) On Thursday morning, in the waiting lounge of the opening ceremony of the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai, two hours before the ceremony began, the guests had already begun arriving. They took selfies, chatted, posed for group photos with old friends and gave interviews to the media. According to on-site observations by the Global Times, in the relaxing atmosphere, the words they mentioned most were "opportunity," "openness" and "market." Running from Thursday to next Tuesday, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, with a total exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters. Over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debut at the event, the highest number in history. US exhibitors occupy more than 50,000 square meters, leading for the eighth consecutive year, while companies from Germany, the UK and France also rank among the top participants. Jim Sutter, CEO of the US Soybean Export Counci, is among the first batch of representatives of American soybean exporters. "We've been doing work in China since 1982, so 44 years history here. And I think the CIIE has become such a big event, and it's just something you can't miss. If you're doing business in China, you need to be at the CIIE," Sutter told the Global Times. Valuing the Chinese market and embracing new cooperation opportunities is a shared sentiment among many representatives present. "China is a very, a very good market for Moldova products. Moldova is a big wine producer. We have the biggest wine sellers in the world, and we hope to have a bigger market in China to sell this wine and to have Chinese consumers buy a wine. So why not give Chinese consumers more choice in regards to this?" said Claudiu Nasui, Minister of Economic Development and Digitalization of Moldova. China accounts for 30 percent of Shiseido's global market share, and China is one of the most important markets for us. With 45 years presence in China, we are continuing to bring new innovations here. We deeply understand Chinese consumers and will identify opportunities to create together with local Chinese consumers," said Toshinobu Umetsu, CEO of Shiseido China and Travel Retail Region. A report released by Beijing Normal University and the China Association for International Trade on Wednesday said China's position as an important export destination for countries around the world is becoming increasingly prominent. From 2001 to 2025, the share of global exports to China in total global exports showed an overall steady upward trend, rising from 3.91 percent in 2001 to 10.49 percent in 2024. In 2025, the share of global exports to China in total global exports was 9.79 percent. It exceeded 9 percent for the first time in 2010 and has generally remained above 10.5 percent since 2018. This indicates that China's status as a major global export destination continues to be consolidated, the report said. "CIIE is important to learn about what the Chinese market needs and also to identify what are the things that developing countries can do to access the Chinese market. So my expectations for next year is that this company continues to grow and that more countries can participate in the Chinese market," Luz Ma de la Mora, director of UNCTAD's Division on International Trade and Commodities, told the Global Times on Thursday. "Chinese companies can also help developing countries to integrate into their supply chains, not only for the market Chinese market, but also for the global markets," Mora said.

item.title: Harnessing desert sun: Chinese firms help advance UAE's clean energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 12:31:00
This undated drone photo shows a view of the 1.5-gigawatt Abu Dhabi PV3 Al Ajban solar project in northeastern Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates. With a Chinese company involved in its construction, the project is nearing grid connection, highlighting the growing China-UAE partnership in advancing the transition to low-carbon energy. (Power Construction Corporation of China/Handout via Xinhua) Under the bright desert sun, rows of photovoltaic panels stretch toward the horizon, their steel mounts casting parallel shadows on pale-yellow sand. The vast solar array is part of the 1.5-gigawatt Abu Dhabi PV3 Al Ajban solar project in northeastern Abu Dhabi. With a Chinese company involved in its construction, the project is nearing grid connection, highlighting the growing China-UAE partnership in advancing the transition to low-carbon energy. Inside the substation area, electrical equipment of different sizes stands in orderly rows, while workers in helmets and reflective vests are completing the remaining construction work. "Once completed, the plant is expected to generate 4.4 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually, enough for about 160,000 households," said Wang Xinjin, project manager with Power Construction Corporation of China, or PowerChina. The project is expected to cut carbon dioxide emissions by around 2.4 million tonnes each year, supporting the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in expanding its clean energy supply and advancing its low-carbon transition, Wang added. Spanning about 20 square km, the project is PowerChina's first large-scale solar power project in the kingdom. PowerChina's Huadong Engineering Corporation Limited is responsible for its engineering, procurement, and construction. Chinese-made photovoltaic installation robots have also been deployed at the site, bringing greater automation to module installation. From solar panels to intelligent construction equipment, China's renewable-energy advances are increasingly being applied in energy infrastructure projects across the Gulf region. The UAE has accelerated renewable energy development in recent years to diversify its energy mix and has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Several solar and wind projects involving Chinese companies have begun operations, harnessing the country's abundant sunshine and wind resources to generate clean electricity. In the desert south of Dubai, phases four and five of the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park present different approaches to converting sunlight into electricity. The fourth phase, built by Shanghai Electric Group, combines 700 MW of concentrated solar power with 250 MW of photovoltaic capacity. Its thermal storage system stores some collected solar energy for use after sunset. The project is expected to cut carbon emissions by about 1.6 million tonnes annually. Shanghai Electric also participated in the fifth phase, a 900-MW photovoltaic project now in operation, expected to reduce carbon emissions by about 1.18 million tonnes per year. Together, the two projects can cut emissions by about 2.78 million tonnes annually. Chinese companies are also helping the UAE explore renewable energy sources beyond solar power. The UAE Wind Program, the country's first utility-scale wind power project, was completed by PowerChina in 2023, with wind farms spanning islands, mountainous terrain and semi-desert landscapes. The project can serve more than 23,000 households each year and cut carbon emissions by around 120,000 tonnes annually. Meanwhile, as renewable energy capacity expands, ensuring a reliable power supply has become a major challenge, prompting China-UAE cooperation to move beyond stand-alone solar projects to integrated photovoltaic and large-scale energy storage projects. In Abu Dhabi, PowerChina is in the construction of a major solar and battery storage project designed to provide clean electricity around the clock. The northern section undertaken by the Chinese side includes 2.1 GW of direct-current photovoltaic capacity and a 7.75-gigawatt-hour battery energy storage system, designed to provide clean electricity around the clock and cut emissions by about 5.7 million tonnes annually once operational. Francesco La Camera, director-general of the International Renewable Energy Agency, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that China has made important contributions to the global energy transition by advancing technology and lowering the cost of clean energy equipment, making clean energy more affordable and accessible. Stronger cooperation in technology, financing and infrastructure could enable more countries to benefit from falling renewable energy costs and accelerate global emissions reduction, he said. item.title: The Democrats have won, but Europe shouldn't rush to pop the champagne
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 11:38:00
Illustration: Liu Rui/GT As the Democratic Party swept both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, many in Europe felt "relieved." German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius was quick to congratulate the Democrats on a "historic victory." European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose expressed hope that this could improve transatlantic relations, citing support for Ukraine and the green transition as areas where the election results could have a positive impact. Politico.eu published an article titled "The blue tsunami sparks joy, hope and mockery in Europe." It is not hard to understand why some Europeans feel this way. Over the past two years, Europe has endured plenty of grievances at the hands of the US - whether it was Washington's barely concealed coveting of Greenland, its exploitation of Europe in trade disputes or its "stab in the back" regarding the Ukraine issue. The cracks in the transatlantic alliance have grown deeper, and Europe's disappointment with the US is written all over its face. But even so, at the strategic level, Europe still clings desperately to a last shred of illusion: If the White House changes its leadership, perhaps US-Europe relations can return to the way they once were. But this illusion is precisely Europe's fatal weakness and the root of the various predicaments it faces today. Even if the White House changes hands and the Democrats return to power, will things really be better for Europe? No. Don't forget that it was during the Biden administration that the Ukraine crisis was exploited to create conflict, causing Europe to "bleed" and then turning around to "drain" Europe. The hegemonic nature and extreme selfishness of Washington's foreign policy have never changed with the rotation of parties. Europe, unable to see this clearly, will only find its list of protection fees growing longer and longer, and the imbalance in its external economic and security power will only become more severe. Europe tying its own future to the US as a "savior" essentially reflects a dependence on the Western-centric order. It is under this dependence that Europe, lacking strategic autonomy, has increasingly become a political dwarf. This is quite sad. The EU, with the collective strength of 27 countries, is one of the world's largest single markets; it should be one of the economies most confident in standing on equal footing with the US. Yet, in the face of US bullying and extortion, as well as the inflaming of tensions in its own neighborhood, Europe dares not "irritate the US" and willingly "makes concessions piece by piece in exchange for temporary relief." Many European elites always anesthetize themselves with the term "security," but what geopolitical security does an EU, whose economy and industry are being gradually drained, still need? In recent years, in order to maintain the "dignity" of the transatlantic alliance, Europe has swallowed its grievances and paid an extremely high price. To align with the US on Russia policy, Europe's energy structure and manufacturing landscape have undergone turmoil. In its attempt to keep pace with the US in the tech cold war, European industry has missed many development opportunities. Strategically, Europe has been bound step by step to the US strategic chariot and has never been able to handle relations with other countries in a normal posture. If it continues to cling to the belief that "relying on Atlantic cooperation can preserve the old order," Europe will sooner or later pay an even higher price for this dependency. The Democrats have won, but Europe shouldn't rush to pop the champagne.

item.title: Seeds of unity, prosperity take root in Xinjiang's Pomegranate Lane
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 11:18:00
Ablekim Musa (L) and Zhou Jinshan talk in Daxi Village, Yuli County, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Yuetikeer Nijiati/Xinhua) With the cotton-picking season underway in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China, Zhou Jinshan, 62, has already finished machine-harvesting his own fields. However, his work is far from over. After arranging a machine for his neighbor, Ablekim Musa, to harvest cotton, Zhou plans to send another machine to deep-plow the Uygur farmer's fields as winter approaches, preparing the land for spring sowing next year. For Zhou, helping Ablekim comes naturally. "We are as close as brothers, even closer than real brothers," he said. Zhou and Ablekim live in Pomegranate Lane in Daxi Village of Yuli County. Stretching about 800 meters, this lane accommodates 18 households from both the Han and Uygur ethnic groups and has long been celebrated for the warm relationships among its residents. China is home to 56 ethnic groups, including the Han and 55 ethnic minorities that collectively account for nearly one-tenth of the country's population, according to the latest national census. In China, the image of pomegranate seeds clustered closely together often symbolizes unity among ethnic groups. The lane in Daxi Village takes its name from this familiar metaphor. For Zhou and Ablekim, this name is not an aspiration yet to be fulfilled, but a reality they have lived for years. Their friendship began around two decades ago, when Zhou's car got stuck in a remote area. Ablekim, who happened to be passing by on his bicycle, helped lift Zhou out of danger. After becoming neighbors in Pomegranate Lane, the two grew even closer. Drawing on his rich experience in cotton farming, Zhou offered Ablekim hands-on guidance at every stage of cotton production. "Zhou taught me everything he knew," said Ablekim. "With his help, I've expanded my cotton fields from 20 mu (1.33 hectares) to over 100 mu, and the cotton yield per mu has also increased significantly." The support, notably, has gone both ways. Last year, when Zhou's orchard was hit by disease, Ablekim immediately rallied fellow villagers in the lane to help prune affected branches and save the trees. In their spare time, the two farmers often visit each other's homes, chatting about everything from the latest developments in agricultural technology to family matters. Such neighborly ties are part of everyday life in Pomegranate Lane. "People in Pomegranate Lane live by a simple rule: when there's naan bread, we eat together, and when there's hardship, we stand together," Zhou said. A tradition has also taken root among the lane's residents. During the Spring Festival, they gather for a hearty meal to celebrate China's most important traditional holiday and exchange best wishes for the year ahead. Xatgul Rahman, Party chief of Daxi Village, describes Pomegranate Lane as a microcosm of the village's ethnic unity. In recent years, the village has promoted a regular pairing program to strengthen ties among residents of different ethnic groups, with 318 pairs formed so far. The story of Pomegranate Lane has also attracted growing attention beyond the village and brought in more visitors. The villagers often welcome them into their homes, sharing their experiences of living and working together. "We are proud to share our stories and help more people understand our hometown," Xatgul said. Zhou sees the influx of visitors as an opportunity to boost his income. He is already considering opening a homestay -- with Ablekim as his business partner, of course. "Just as the lane's name suggests, we will stick together tightly like pomegranate seeds to build businesses and create a better future," Zhou noted.

item.title: 464 Chinese peacekeepers in Lebanon awarded UN medals of peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 11:16:00
A medal parade ceremony is held at the Chinese peacekeepers' camp in Hanniyah village, southern Lebanon, Nov. 3, 2026. A total of 464 peacekeepers of the 24th Chinese peacekeeping contingent to Lebanon were awarded UN medals of peace on Tuesday for their commitment to maintaining stability and peace in the south of the country. A medal parade ceremony was held at the Chinese peacekeepers' camp in Hanniyah village in southern Lebanon to honor the Chinese peacekeeping contingent, part of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). (Photo by Ali Hashisho/Xinhua) A total of 464 peacekeepers of the 24th Chinese peacekeeping contingent to Lebanon were awarded UN medals of peace on Tuesday for their commitment to maintaining stability and peace in the south of the country. A medal parade ceremony was held at the Chinese peacekeepers' camp in Hanniyah village in southern Lebanon to honor the Chinese peacekeeping contingent, part of the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL). In his address at the event, Diodato Abagnara, UNIFIL head of mission and force commander, praised the Chinese peacekeepers for their prompt response, practical solutions and decisive action, describing them as "problem-solvers" who could be "a real game changer for the mission" when time mattered most. The 24th Chinese peacekeeping contingent, which includes a multi-functional engineer detachment, a construction engineer detachment and a medical detachment, has been serving the UN Mission since December 2025. To date, the Chinese peacekeepers have cleared more than 825 square meters of minefields, safely removed over 146 landmines, and provided medical treatments to above 3,400 UNIFIL personnel and local people. More than 8,800 Chinese peacekeepers have been dispatched to Lebanon since 2006. UNIFIL was first established in 1978 to confirm Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon. After the 2006 war between Hezbollah and Israel, UNIFIL's mandate was expanded by UN Security Council Resolution 1701 to monitor the cessation of hostilities and to accompany the deployment of Lebanese armed forces throughout southern Lebanon as Israel withdrew its troops. In August 2025, the Security Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for the final time until Dec. 31, 2026, with a drawdown and withdrawal to follow within one year. item.title: When Singles' Day shoppers start stocking up on AI tokens, the time has changed: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05 00:30:00
Concept picture of Token Photo: VCG As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." This year's Double 11, or Singles' Day, shopping festival has brought a new item to Chinese consumers' shopping lists: Token. Tmall and JD.com have each introduced AI token sections bringing together services from Alibaba Cloud, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Zhipu AI. One livestream even recorded sales of 2 trillion tokens in just half an hour. The fact that AI tokens have become one of the headline products on e-commerce platforms is a phenomenon rarely seen anywhere else in the world. Foreign media have taken notice, expressing both curiosity and astonishment. There was a time when Americans were driving cars, watching television and eating fried chicken, while the "four big things" in Chinese households were watches, bicycles, sewing machines and radios. It was not until the late 1970s that televisions, refrigerators and washing machines began to find their way into a limited number of Chinese homes. In those days, the West had the power to set the standard for what constituted "modern living," and its way of life was widely regarded as the model for the future. China's priority was to catch up with industrialization, bringing within reach of ordinary households products that had long been commonplace elsewhere. Few could have imagined that, decades later, China would be at the forefront of the widespread adoption of smart devices, mobile payments and digital services. Fewer even could have predicted that China would become a force in defining new forms of consumption, new standards and even new ways of life in the latest wave of digital transformation. The same transformation is also unfolding in digital technology. A new digital product or concept would often first take shape in Silicon Valley before gradually spreading to the rest of the world. But the appearance of tokens on Singles' Day shopping shelves has challenged this long-established pattern. Tokens are no longer simply another overseas concept or business model replicated in China. Instead, the token-based consumption has emerged from the combined forces of China's vast digital consumer market, highly active user base and mature industrial ecosystem. Just a few years ago, some Western commentators were still quick to question China's capacity for digital innovation, arguing that it could make only incremental advances in applications but would never forge its own path in foundational technologies. Yet the rapid uptake of open-source large language models, the gradual deployment of humanoid robots in industrial settings, and now the arrival of digital resources in the mass consumer market tell a different story. The world is witnessing an innovation hub capable of continually defining new demands and creating new applications. As ordinary Chinese consumers embrace AI and enjoy the convenience of stockpiling tokens through e-commerce livestreams, and as humanoid robots and green manufacturing emerge as new showcases of China's intelligent manufacturing capabilities and Chinese modernization, an increasing number of Western media outlets and scholars are coming to recognize a remarkable reality: "The future is in China." Today, AI is not only directly driving consumption of smart devices and related hardware, but the "AI Plus" initiative is also deeply empowering the rapid development of sectors such as education, healthcare, elderly care, culture and tourism, employment, and consumer services. As AI enters millions of households and empowers thousands of industries, a more competitive AI consumer ecosystem will bring more affordable tokens and a wider range of application scenarios. Underpinning this transformation is China's rapid progress in AI foundation models, cloud computing, and the chip application ecosystem. China is developing distinctive competitive advantages in the global AI race. According to OpenRouter, a global AI model aggregation platform, Chinese large language models have outpaced their US counterparts in token usage for 27 consecutive weeks, including the week of October 26 to November 1. More than one-third of the tokens used by enterprises in the Global South countries come from Chinese models. Increasingly, the decisive factor in AI competition is whether companies can consistently deliver reliable, practical AI services to businesses and consumers at reasonable costs, and whether technological advances can be translated into productivity gains across industries. Why has China been among the first to develop an ecosystem for token consumption? The answer is simple: the public's high level of acceptance has accelerated the development of the ecosystem, while a mature ecosystem has, in turn, further reinforced positive public attitudes. A 2025 KPMG survey covering 47 countries found that Chinese people were among the most optimistic about AI. From electronic payments to e-commerce and food delivery, from short videos to intelligent driving, and now to access to highly cost-effective AI tokens, Chinese consumers have undoubtedly been at the forefront of enjoying the benefits of the intelligent era. This positive, self-reinforcing ecosystem is the natural outcome of China's remarkable rise in comprehensive national strength and the broad improvement in its population's educational and cultural attainment over the past several decades. From the "four big things" and "three big things" that once symbolized household prosperity to the integration of digital technologies into everyday consumption today, the Chinese people's pursuit of a better life has never changed. What has changed is our ability and approach to fulfill that aspiration. Today, we are turning the possibilities of a new era of digital civilization into experiences that benefit billions of people globally. This transformation has not been driven by exploitation, coercion, or the erection of barriers, but by practical efforts to ensure that ordinary people can genuinely and equally share in the benefits of technological progress.

item.title: GT Voice: Why resisting US pressure matters for South Korean chipmakers
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 22:26:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG Washington's efforts to attract South Korean chip investment risk being undermined by its own restrictions. Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that US officials have held up approval for American chipmaking equipment needed by SK hynix to expand its production in China, complicating the South Korean chipmaker's plans for new memory-chip plants in the state of New York. According to Reuters, SK hynix is seeking US export licenses to equip its plant in Dalian, Northeast China's Liaoning Province, arguing that increased production there would help fund its planned US expansion. Negotiations are ongoing, with the outcome uncertain. But the episode already exposes tension in US-South Korea chip "cooperation." Washington wants to attract more South Korean investment and manufacturing capacity to the US, while its export controls constrain South Korean chipmakers' ability to expand its production in China. This reveals a divergence of interests: Washington is seeking to strengthen its own semiconductor industry, even at the potential expense of South Korean companies' commercial interests. For a fuller picture of the pressure facing South Korean chipmakers, a September report by The Korea Herald is worth revisiting. It said that Washington had revived its push for targeted semiconductor tariffs, raising pressure on Samsung Electronics and SK hynix to expand US production or face duties on chips made overseas. If South Korean chipmakers expand their US operations under such pressure, a growing share of investment, advanced manufacturing capacity and high-value jobs could accrue to the US rather than South Korea. This raises a question about whether such "cooperation" truly serves both sides' interests. Washington stands to gain new investment and jobs, while South Korean companies face constraints on their global operations and risk seeing more of their industrial capabilities move overseas. The arrangement appears to put US industrial interests first, leaving South Korea to bear much of the commercial and strategic cost. On its US investment plans, South Korean media outlet AJP reported on Wednesday that SK hynix had yet to finalize any specific plans for new semiconductor manufacturing facilities in the US. SK hynix also said that it was continuing to bring US-made semiconductor manufacturing equipment into its Dalian plant under an existing export license, while negotiations over next year's authorization remain underway, AJP reported. Why are these Chinese factories so important to South Korean chipmakers? The Korea JoongAng Daily reported in August that SK hynix's plant in Wuxi, East China's Jiangsu Province, accounts for 40 percent of its total dynamic random-access memory output, while its Dalian plant accounts for 30 percent of its total NAND output. At a time of strong global demand and tight memory-chip supply, China's production capacity is a valuable asset for South Korean chipmakers. Retaining access to this capacity is plainly in the commercial interests of these companies. China's value also lies in its mature industrial ecosystem. Its extensive supplier networks and manufacturing capabilities have long supported South Korean chipmakers' global operations. This has been a mutually beneficial arrangement, with South Korean companies drawing on China's industrial base while contributing investment to the wider supply chain. Yet Washington is putting South Korean chipmakers in a difficult position. While seeking to attract their investment to the US, it is also trying to limit their ability to expand production in China. In doing so, Washington is putting its geopolitical objectives ahead of South Korean companies' commercial interests. South Korean chipmakers should not accommodate US demands at the expense of their global operations. They have every reason to preserve the flexibility to make investment and production decisions based on commercial considerations. China's semiconductor industry is advancing rapidly, creating new competitive pressures for South Korean chipmakers. But competition does not preclude cooperation where interests remain aligned. The question is whether South Korean chipmakers can withstand US pressure without sacrificing the global reach and commercial flexibility on which their competitiveness depends. That balance will have consequences well beyond their operations in China.
